chunks: Trade-offs of integration. The question: What are some tradeoffs of integration?
Putting more functions on one chip brings them close together. That saves energy, speeds things up and shrinks the product. But it has costs.
Big chips are far more likely to be ruined by a tiny flaw, so the cost of each working chip climbs fast.
Different functions also want different manufacturing recipes, noisy circuits disturb sensitive ones, and heat gathers in one spot.
The modern fix is to split a big design into smaller chips in one package.
Imagine cutting shirts from a cloth that has random stains. A small shirt panel is often clean. A huge panel almost always catches a stain, and you throw away the whole piece.
A wafer, the round slice of silicon that chips are cut from, works the same way: every flaw ruins the chip it lands on.
The cloth picture does not cover noise or heat, which are separate costs of putting things together.
Cost per good die is convex in area. Going from 100 to 600 mm² multiplies area by 6 but cost by about 12 at D0 = 0.
1, and by far more at the higher defect density of a young process (red).
This is the economic pressure behind chiplets and the reason that early in a node's life only small dies are built.
Die: one chip's piece of silicon, cut from a wafer. Defect: a tiny flaw that ruins any die it lands on. Yield: the fraction of dies that come out good.
Cost per good die: the wafer's cost divided by the number of good dies. Chiplet: a small die made to share one package (the protective case around chips) with others.
Respin: a new version of the chip made to fix a bug.
A wafer costs 10,000 USD, and flaws average 0. 1 per square centimeter. A 100 mm² die gets 640 dies per wafer, and about 90. 5% are good in a standard simple model.
That is roughly 579 good dies, or about 17 USD each. A 600 mm² die gets only 91 dies, and about 54. 9% are good. That is roughly 50 good dies, or about 200 USD each.
Six times the area costs about 12 times as much. That is the whole idea.
"Integration gives lower energy, higher bandwidth, lower latency and smaller, cheaper systems.

The costs: yield drops with die area so cost per good die rises faster than linearly; one process can't suit logic, analog, RF and memory; digital noise couples into sensitive blocks; heat concentrates; and verification, NRE and respin risk grow.
Chiplets are the modern compromise: smaller dies in the best process, joined by advanced packaging."
